cleanIntro: This guide comes from Browning's own owner's manual for the BLR, the lever-action rifle with a rack-and-pinion lever, a rotating multi-lug bolt and a detachable box magazine, made in short-action, long-action and magnum calibers and as a takedown model. It has no separate manual safety: the folding hammer and its half-cock position are how the rifle is carried. The field strip is short: lever down, magazine out, bolt left open so the bore can be cleaned from the muzzle. Browning's book stops there and says not to take the rifle any further apart.

steps.title: Lever down: the chamber empties
steps.action: Point the muzzle somewhere safe and keep your fingers off the trigger. Swing the finger lever all the way down; that opens the bolt and extracts and ejects any cartridge in the chamber. Leave the lever down. The BLR has no manual safety, so a safe muzzle and a finger off the trigger are what keep this step safe.
steps.quote: Carefully remove any cartridge in the chamber by swinging the finger lever downward.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Unloading, step 1
steps.warn: WHEN UNLOADING YOUR RIFLE, ALWAYS KEEP YOUR FINGERS AWAY FROM THE TRIGGER.

steps.title: Magazine out, with the lever still down
steps.action: With the lever still in the down position, press down on the magazine release button with your index finger and slide the magazine out of its recess. Doing it with the lever down means closing the lever cannot feed another cartridge. Taking the magazine out does not make the rifle safe on its own: a cartridge in the chamber can still fire without it.
steps.quote: With the lever in the down position, remove the magazine from the rifle.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Unloading, step 2
steps.warn: REMOVING THE MAGAZINE FROM THE RIFLE DOES NOT PREVENT THE RIFLE FROM BEING FIRED.

steps.title: Look into the chamber
steps.action: With the bolt open, look into the chamber yourself and make sure no cartridge is left there; do not rely on hearing one eject. Then look at the bore and the magazine well too. Only a chamber you have actually seen empty counts as empty.
steps.quote: Inspect the chamber to ensure all cartridges have been removed from the rifle.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Unloading, step 3
steps.warn: ALWAYS INSPECT THE CHAMBER, BARREL AND MAGAZINE CAREFULLY AFTER UNLOADING TO BE SURE ALL LIVE CARTRIDGES ARE CLEARED FROM THE FIREARM.

steps.title: Empty the magazine; ammunition off the bench
steps.action: Push each cartridge forward with your thumb until it slides out past the lips of the magazine. Count them out until the magazine is empty. Then put all the ammunition away from where you are going to clean, so nothing live ends up back in the rifle by mistake.
steps.quote: Cartridges in the magazine may be removed by sliding them forward and out of the magazine with the thumb.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Unloading, step 4
steps.warn: KEEP ALL AMMUNITION AWAY FROM THE CLEANING AREA.

steps.title: Lever down, ejection port open, bolt back
steps.action: Before cleaning, check the three things Browning asks for: chamber and magazine empty, lever down, ejection port open. With the lever down the bolt is open, which lets the rod and patch go all the way through the bore and partly into the receiver. Leave the rifle like this for the cleaning.
steps.quote: Be certain the chamber and magazine are completely unloaded, the lever is down, and the ejection port is open.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 1

steps.title: Field strip complete
steps.action: On the bench now: the rifle with its lever down and bolt open, and the empty magazine. That is the whole field strip for the BLR. The bolt and lever stay in the rifle, and the bore is cleaned from the muzzle with the bolt open. Browning's book takes the rifle no further apart than this.
steps.quote: Place the bolt in the open position to allow the rod and patch to go completely through the bore and partly into the receiver.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 2

steps.title: Rod and patch in from the muzzle, with a rod guide
steps.action: Fit a muzzle rod guide, and use a cleaning rod with a slotted tip or a jag and a patch big enough to fit the bore snugly. Put the rod in at the muzzle and run it back and forth several times. Keep the rod and its handle off the crown of the muzzle: damage there can spoil the rifle's accuracy.
steps.quote: Insert the rod and patch into the barrel at the muzzle end and run back and forth several times.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 2

steps.title: Heavy fouling: brass brush, pushed all the way through
steps.action: Some powder residue is normal and usually comes out with a patch soaked in nitro solvent. If the fouling is heavy, dip a brass bore brush in nitro solvent and scrub the chamber and bore until it is gone. Push the brush all the way out of the barrel before you pull it back, so the bristles do not break off.
steps.quote: To prevent brass bristles from breaking off, the brush should be pushed completely through the bore before being withdrawn.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 3

steps.title: Copper solvent for the jacket fouling
steps.action: For best accuracy Browning recommends a copper solvent too, because copper and zinc from bullet jackets stick to the barrel. Swab the bore with it following the solvent maker's own procedure. Work with good ventilation and eye protection, and keep solvent away from any flame.
steps.quote: Swab the bore of your rifle with a good copper solvent using the manufacturer’s recommended procedure.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 4

steps.title: Dry the bore, then one slightly oiled patch
steps.action: When the fouling is out, wipe the bore dry. Then push one slightly oiled patch through to protect it, using a fine, light gun oil. Look through the barrel afterward to make sure no patch or anything else has been left in the bore.
steps.quote: Then, pass a slightly oiled patch through the bore for preservation.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 5

steps.title: Brush out the receiver, a light film of oil on moving parts
steps.action: Use a small brush or a rag to get dirt out of the receiver and the rest of the action. Then lightly oil the moving parts with a good lightweight gun oil; a very light film is enough. Do not pour oil in: it drains down into the wood, softens it and loosens the stock for good, and too much oil can also stop the rifle working properly.
steps.quote: Lightly lubricate all moving parts with a high-quality, lightweight gun oil.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, step 6
steps.warn: DO NOT POUR LARGE QUANTITIES OF OIL INTO THE RECEIVER OR OTHER PARTS.

steps.title: Do not take the rifle any further apart
steps.action: The bolt, lever and trigger stay in the rifle. Browning calls the rifle a specialized, finely fitted mechanism that can be permanently damaged by trying to take the inner assemblies apart, and says the trigger should only be adjusted by a qualified gunsmith. If it needs more than this, Browning sends you to a qualified gunsmith or its service facility in Arnold, Missouri.
steps.quote: NEVER ATTEMPT TO TAKE YOUR FIREARM APART FURTHER THAN EXPLAINED IN THIS OWNER’S MANUAL.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions

no.q: NEVER ATTEMPT TO TAKE YOUR FIREARM APART FURTHER THAN EXPLAINED IN THIS OWNER’S MANUAL.
no.src: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions

steps.title: Spray the magazine inside and out, then dry it
steps.action: Browning says to check the magazine often and normally clean it every 500 to 1000 rounds, because oil and dirt build up inside. Wear eye protection. Spray it inside and out with an aerosol solvent that will not harm or corrode its parts, shake out the excess, and dry it with a cloth or compressed air.
steps.quote: Clean the magazine by spraying it both inside and out with an aerosol solvent that will not adversely affect or corrode the components.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING THE MAGAZINE, steps 2-3
steps.warn: WEAR EYE PROTECTION WHEN CLEANING THE MAGAZINE TO PREVENT SOLVENTS OR OTHER AGENTS FROM CONTACTING YOUR EYES, RESULTING IN INJURY.

steps.title: A very thin coat of oil, wiped off again
steps.action: Wipe off any dirt or residue left on the magazine. Put on a very thin coat of oil, then wipe it clean again so only a trace remains. A wet magazine collects grit, which is exactly what the cleaning took out.
steps.quote: Wipe off any dirt or residue, then apply a very thin coat of oil and wipe clean again.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING THE MAGAZINE, step 4

steps.title: Oiled cloth on the metal, oil or wax on the wood
steps.action: Wipe all the exposed metal with an oiled cloth, getting every finger mark, because moisture collects in them. Give the metal a light film of oil whenever the rifle has been out in bad weather or handled a lot. Wood can be wiped with a light gun oil or polished with a good furniture wax, but use one or the other, not both.
steps.quote: Wipe all exposed metal surfaces with an oiled cloth, making sure to wipe the gun clean of all finger marks.
steps.cite: Browning BLR Rifle Owner's Manual — UNKNOWN — not printed in the document (document code 24-BFA-097 on the closing lines) — Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions > CLEANING PROCEDURES, steps 7-8

deepAbsentReason: Browning's BLR book ends at the field strip, with the lever down, the bolt open and the magazine out, and forbids going further: under Cleaning and Maintenance Suggestions it says "NEVER ATTEMPT TO TAKE YOUR FIREARM APART FURTHER THAN EXPLAINED IN THIS OWNER’S MANUAL." and sends any further disassembly to a qualified gunsmith or its Arnold, Missouri service facility. The book's only other separation, under Takedown Models, splits a takedown rifle into two halves for transport and is not part of its cleaning procedure. There is no deeper procedure to follow.

cleaning.name: BORE & CHAMBER
tasks: Lever down and bolt open, so the rod goes all the way through
Muzzle rod guide, and a patch big enough to fit snugly
Do not let the rod or its handle strike the crown of the muzzle
Normal residue: a patch soaked in nitro solvent
Heavy fouling: brass brush with nitro solvent, pushed all the way through before it comes back
Copper solvent for jacket fouling, used the way its maker says
Bore wiped dry, then one slightly oiled patch
Check that nothing is left in the bore

cleaning.name: RECEIVER & ACTION
tasks: Dirt out of the receiver and the action with a small brush or rag
Moving parts lightly oiled; a very light film is enough
Do not pour oil into the action; it drains into the wood and loosens the stock
Never take the rifle apart further than the magazine and an open bolt
Do not adjust the trigger; that is a gunsmith's job

cleaning.name: MAGAZINE
tasks: Check it often; clean it normally every 500 to 1000 rounds
Eye protection on
Aerosol solvent inside and out, excess shaken out, dried with a cloth or air
A very thin coat of oil, then wiped clean again

cleaning.name: EXTERIOR & WOOD
tasks: All exposed metal wiped with an oiled cloth, finger marks included
Wood: light gun oil or furniture wax, not both
Keep solvents, insect repellent and sunscreen off the finishes

reassembly: Make sure the chamber and magazine are empty and no ammunition is on the bench.
Look through the bore once more to be sure no patch or other obstruction is left in it.
Swing the finger lever completely upward to close the bolt.
Push the empty magazine into the rifle until it is retained; a sharp, metallic click tells you it has engaged the magazine latch.
Lower the hammer to the half-cock position and fold it forward, the position Browning recommends for handling and storage.
fncheck: With the rifle empty and pointed somewhere safe, swing the finger lever completely down and back up a few times and feel the bolt open and close smoothly; the hammer is cocked when the lever closes. Browning's trigger cannot be pulled until the lever is fully closed. Lower the hammer the way the book describes: thumb on the hammer to hold it back, squeeze the trigger only until the hammer leaves full cock, take your finger off the trigger, then ease the hammer down into the half-cock notch and fold it forward. Do not snap the hammer on an empty chamber. Press the magazine release, check the magazine slides out freely, and push it back until it clicks home. Never test the rifle's function with live ammunition.
